text:
The college sat on a hill above a town with a river, a train station that no longer served trains, and a population that declined each autumn with the regularity of a tide. I arrived in October with a duffel bag, a library card I had made myself at nineteen, and the conviction that I was finally going to be someone nobody had a theory about.

Small colleges are built out of other people's opinions. Within a month, a version of me circulated in the dining hall and the Barn's back room, where the coffee was the color of dishwater: a girl from a mid-sized city, sharp, funny, a little guarded, interested in nobody in particular. It was a good version. It was a version I had not written.

Carl wrote over it first.

He was a history major with a laugh that started before the joke finished, so that by the time it did, everyone was laughing with him. He told stories the way other people ate. In November he asked me to dinner at the Old Wharf, which everyone agreed was overpriced, and he ordered the lamb and I ordered the same, because I was twenty-one and believed matching orders was a form of intimacy. He was kind in the way that makes kindness seem like a personality trait. He remembered things I mentioned once, in passing, my mother's garden, my fear of being a fraud, and returned them to me later as gifts.

Martin came in December, driving from the city with my old best friend's cousin's car, arriving with borrowed machinery and the unshakable sense that my life required his presence in it. Martin had loved me since sophomore year in a way he never once said out loud, which was itself a kind of saying. He rented a room above the laundromat on Ferry Street, sat in my seminar taking notes he never needed, and took my table in the Barn whether I was coming or not.

I told myself Martin was a friend, with a specificity that frightened me, because I could hear the sentence being prepared in advance, like a card held to the light.

The seminar was on modern poetry, taught by a man who wore the same tweed jacket for two years running and said, in the first week, that the only dishonesty in a poem is the one the reader accepts. I enrolled because the Thursday two o'clock slot was empty and the room had a radiator that clicked like a metronome, and because I wanted, absurdly, to be somewhere where honesty was the stated curriculum.

Johan was in it. He was Dutch, or had the Dutchness of a name and a manner, and he read in the back row with his eyes moving so fast it looked like memorizing, which, I would learn, was what he was doing. He spoke perhaps twice per class, and when he did, he said things like: "The poet is lying to the audience and also to himself, and the poem is only the lie he believes." The room would go quiet. Nobody argued with Johan, because he never made claims that could be met. He just kept removing the furniture and leaving you standing in the open.

I wanted his attention the way you want a window in a room where you have slept with your eyes shut.

Carl and I became what the Old Wharf would have called a couple, though Carl preferred the word "us," which meant whatever he needed it to mean that week. He put his hand on the small of my back in public and took my hand in private, as though privacy made the gesture safer. In February, when the river froze and the town turned the color of a bruise, he told me he had never felt like that before, and I believed him, because believing was the one thing I had always been very good at.

Lizzy was a sociology major who had known Carl since freshman orientation. She sat with me at the Barn on Thursdays when Martin was away, and she was direct in the way Carl was not, which made her dangerous. In the second week of March she set down her coffee, cold, because Lizzy always got cold coffee and never went back for it, and she said, "He's been seeing me since October."

She looked at the Barn's ceiling, where a water stain was shaped like the state of Maine.

"I don't understand why I'm telling you this," she said. "You're not my problem."

It was the kindest sentence she ever spoke to me and the most honest, and those two things were not, in her case, separate.

I want to say I confronted Carl, but I did something worse: three days of silence, letting him wonder what he had done wrong, because the silence was mine to manage and the explanation was his to earn. This was the thing nobody had ever named. I did not want to be told the truth. I wanted to choose the moment of being told it, so that the darkness would be mine and not his. Carl, to his credit, came to my door on the fourth night and told me about Lizzy himself, surprised, I could see, that he had been forced to say the word and mean it. He was sorry. He was not sorry. He gave me both at once, and I let them stand there.

Martin knew. This is the part I have never told anyone. My best friend watched me be dismantled by a man he had known for two years and said nothing, because he was in love with me, and his silence was his way of being in it. He told me in March at the laundromat, folding my shirts into neat squares, that he had known since November. "I was going to tell you," he said. "I kept waiting for a better time, and then there was you and Carl, and I didn't want to be the thing that ruined it." He said "ruined" the way you say "killed," without drama, because for him it was accurate.

Martin was not a bad man. He had made me the center of his life and could not bear for the center to be shared, and his remedy was withholding, which he believed was loyalty. He said "I'm sorry" and did not come to the Old Wharf for the rest of the year, and I understood, standing at the window of the Barn, that I had done something to him that was not small. He had loved me plainly and I had loved him at a distance, because closeness without management felt to me like a cage, and I had spent my whole life mistaking cages for weather.

What Johan did that spring was smaller and more important than anything. April had come, the hill green in a way that seemed fraudulent after the ice. We were reading a poem about a man who leaves a house without saying goodbye, and the class had agreed the man was a coward, and Johan, who had not spoken in two weeks, said: "The poem isn't about cowardice. It's about a man who has decided that the people in the house will never understand him leaving, and so he stops asking."

The radiator clicked. Everyone looked at him.

I sat there with my notebook open and my pen doing nothing, and understood that he was not reading the poem. He was reading me, and he had read me correctly, and he had done it in front of fourteen people without raising his voice or giving me any way to perform a response. It was the first time anyone had been honest with me without handing me the tools to manage the honesty afterward. It felt like being struck by something soft.

We did not become lovers, and I want to be clear about that, because the version of this story in which the quiet one wins would be a lie, and Johan would have despised a lie. He was lonely in the way of people who have decided that being seen is a risk they will not take twice.

In May I took the bus to the city. The town went by in the usual order: the hill, the river, the dead tracks, the laundromat where Martin had folded shirts into squares I never used. I had not called him. I had not called Lizzy. I had not called Carl, who was by then seeing someone else, or perhaps still Lizzy, or perhaps nothing; I had stopped keeping the ledger, which was the first small act of my own I could remember in years, and I let it feel like nothing, because it was nothing, and the nothing was mine.

Johan had given me a book back in March, poems he said I would understand later. I had put it in the bottom of my duffel and never opened it, because opening it would have felt like an examination, and I was tired of being examined. On the bus I took it out and read the first poem. A woman finally leaves a house. The lines were plain, there was no music in them, she did not look back, and the last line said: *She carried nothing but the key, and used it once, on the way out.*

I did not cry. I read it twice, folded the book, and stood when the driver called my stop, and I did not manage a single thought about how it all went, because it had gone the way it had gone, and I was, at last, the only person left in the room with the door open.

The version of me that circulates now, in the city, in the seminar where I teach, over coffee in a bar nobody agrees is overpriced, is this: a woman who was honest about her own past in a way that still sounds like an apology, and who has stopped, mostly, being told what she is.

I think about Johan sometimes. Martin folding shirts. Carl's laugh arriving early, Lizzy's cold coffee, the radiator marking time for people busy being lied to. I am not sure I was ever lied to, exactly. I was managed, and I liked it, and liking it was the lie, and it was mine, and it took me three years and one frozen river to say that out loud.

The key was small. I still have it.
